summaries.example: Imagine a classmate says, “We should plant flowers near the playground because they make the space nicer for everyone.” The conclusion is “We should plant flowers.” The reason, or premise, is that flowers make the space nicer. To test the argument, ask: Is the reason true? Does it really support the conclusion? Is it enough, or are other facts needed, such as cost and care?
summaries.summary: Informal logic is the study of reasoning as it happens in real life. People use arguments when they explain choices, discuss news, make plans, solve problems, or disagree. An argument is not simply a quarrel. In this subject, it is an attempt to support a point of view with reasons. Informal logic helps us find those reasons and the conclusion they support. It also asks whether the reasons are believable, relevant, and strong enough. Sometimes a speaker leaves a needed reason unstated, so careful readers must identify the missing idea without unfairly changing the argument. Pictures, videos, facial expressions, sounds, tastes, and stories may also carry evidence. The field includes several systems rather than one single method. Some use ideas about fallacies, or common mistakes in reasoning; others use repeating patterns of reasoning called argument schemes. Informal logic is connected with rhetoric, which studies persuasion, and dialectics, which studies exchanges between people. Its larger purpose is to help people understand and assess the arguments that shape everyday life.
key_ideas: Informal logic studies arguments in ordinary conversations, classrooms, news, law, medicine, and public debates.
An argument usually has premises, a conclusion, and a connection called an inference.
Good analysis first makes an argument clear by separating its reasons from its main point.
Words, pictures, sounds, gestures, and stories can all help make an argument.
Different situations have different goals. A debate may seek agreement, while a discussion may seek information or a decision.
There is not just one informal logic. Different systems use different tools for judging arguments.
summaries.why_it_matters: People make important choices using reasons. Informal logic can help you notice whether a claim has support, whether an image is being used fairly, and whether someone has skipped an important assumption. It does not guarantee that everyone will agree, but it gives people better tools for understanding disagreement and explaining their own ideas.

important_terms.definition: A reasoned attempt to support a point of view or answer a disagreement.
A statement offered as a reason for believing another statement.
The main statement that the reasons are meant to support.
The study of how people give and check reasons in everyday life.
A careful look at an argument to see whether its reasons are acceptable, connected, and strong enough.

questions_to_think_about: What reasons support a decision you made today?
Can a picture or video give evidence? What could make it misleading?
When is a criticism of a person relevant to their argument, and when is it just an insult?
What extra information might an argument leave unsaid?

summaries.example: Suppose a student argues: “The school should add more buses because the current routes leave many students waiting for a long time.” To analyze it, first standardize it: premise—current routes create long waits for many students; conclusion—the school should add more buses. The argument also seems to rely on an implicit premise: reducing those waits is an appropriate reason to add buses, and adding buses would probably reduce them. Evaluation then asks whether the premise is supported by reliable information, whether it is relevant, and whether it provides enough support. Evidence about route data, costs, and alternative solutions could strengthen or weaken the case.
summaries.summary: Informal logic (IL) studies reasoning and inference in public discussion, education, interpersonal exchange, law, medicine, and other practical settings. Its central aim is epistemic betterment: arguments should improve belief, understanding, or claims to knowledge by making them more credible. IL therefore develops methods for extracting arguments from ordinary discourse and for assessing their strength. A basic analysis identifies premises, an inference, and a conclusion, but real arguments are often layered, incomplete, rhetorical, visual, or multimodal. Standardization makes their structure clearer by removing irrelevant material, resolving ambiguity, and identifying implicit premises and conclusions. Diagrams can show whether reasons work independently or only together. Systems of IL differ in theoretical background, language, concept of argument, standardization method, and testing tools. Some rely on acceptability, relevance, and sufficiency; others emphasize fallacies, argument schemes, or deductive reconstruction. The entry cautions that no fallacy label settles every case: a personal criticism may reveal bias, and a slippery-slope argument may be well supported. Informal logic is related to rhetoric and dialectics, since arguments must address audiences and respond to opposing views, while also remaining connected to the epistemic question of whether the conclusion is justified. Its broader setting is argumentation theory, which draws on logic, communication, linguistics, psychology, semiotics, artificial intelligence, and other fields.
key_ideas: Informal logic has a normative aim: it develops tools for judging whether real-life arguments are strong, weak, convincing, or unconvincing.
Its basic model includes premises, an inference, and a conclusion, but systems differ over how these elements should be understood and tested.
Standardization removes distracting material, clarifies ambiguous language, and makes implicit premises or conclusions visible. Diagrams can display linked and independent reasons.
Many systems use acceptability, relevance, and sufficiency. Acceptability may involve truth, plausibility, fairness, audience expectations, or the norms of a particular dialogue.

Deductive, inductive, conductive, and abductive forms of support represent different ways premises can bear on conclusions; the entry also discusses attempts to treat informal arguments deductively by adding implicit warrants.
Fallacy labels are useful but not always decisive. Ad hominem criticism, appeals to emotion, and slippery-slope reasoning can sometimes have legitimate roles, depending on context and evidence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Informal logic supplies a bridge between abstract theories of reasoning and the arguments people actually encounter. It helps readers assess claims in speech, writing, images, advertisements, scientific and legal discussion, and digital media without assuming that every argument fits a mathematical template. Because arguments occur in different dialogues and carry different purposes, responsible evaluation requires attention to evidence, hidden assumptions, audience, context, and reasonable objections.

important_terms.definition: The study of reasoning and inference in ordinary language and real-world practices rather than only in highly formal languages.
A claim-reason complex consisting of premises, a conclusion, and an inference connecting them.
The process of restating an argument so its premises, conclusion, inference, and unstated parts are easier to inspect.
An unstated claim needed to connect stated reasons with a conclusion; it is also called a warrant in some analyses.
A broad requirement for good argument: premises should be acceptable, relevant, and sufficient.
A recurring pattern of reasoning, often paired with critical questions for testing it.
A mistake or defective pattern of reasoning; some traditional fallacy forms can nevertheless be reasonable in particular contexts.
A method of support that proposes the best explanation of observed facts.

questions_to_think_about: Should an argument be reconstructed in the most charitable reasonable way, or should analysts avoid adding anything not explicitly stated?
Can an argument be logically strong but rhetorically ineffective for its intended audience?
When does an appeal to authority become reasonable evidence rather than a fallacy?
How should we evaluate visual or multimodal arguments whose meaning depends on images, tone, or gesture?
Do different dialogue goals— inquiry, negotiation, persuasion, or deliberation—require different standards of good argument?

summaries.example: A student says, “Our class should have a longer lunch because many students do not have enough time to eat.” The conclusion is that lunch should be longer. The premise is that many students lack enough eating time. A careful checker asks whether this is based on good evidence, whether it matters to the conclusion, and whether it is enough. The argument may also hide a premise: making lunch longer is a workable way to solve the problem and will not create a larger problem elsewhere. A survey, lunch schedule, and information about other solutions could help test it.
summaries.summary: Informal logic examines how people reason in everyday settings. It looks at arguments in conversations, schoolwork, public debate, news, law, medicine, and many other places. Here, an argument means an attempt to deal with agreement or disagreement by giving evidence for a point of view. The subject asks whether the evidence is acceptable, relevant, and strong enough. It also helps us uncover parts of an argument that are not directly stated. For example, a person may give one reason for a decision while silently assuming that the proposed action will actually solve the problem. Making such assumptions visible allows better evaluation. Informal logic has many systems, not one universal checklist. Some systems study fallacies, while others use argument schemes—common patterns such as reasoning from authority, analogy, example, or a possible chain of consequences. A pattern is not automatically bad; its quality depends on how it is used and what questions it can answer. Informal logic also studies arguments made through pictures, videos, sounds, facial expressions, stories, and other combinations of modes. It connects with rhetoric, which focuses on persuading an audience, and dialectics, which focuses on back-and-forth discussion. The larger field of argumentation theory brings these approaches together and also connects them with communication, psychology, linguistics, and artificial intelligence.
key_ideas: Informal logic is about real-life reasoning, not just classroom puzzles or symbolic formulas.
To understand an argument, separate its premises, conclusion, and inference—the step that connects them.
Arguments can contain missing assumptions. Finding them helps us judge whether the reasoning really works.
A strong argument normally needs acceptable premises, relevant support, and enough support for its conclusion.
Images, videos, tone of voice, gestures, and stories can function as parts of arguments, not just printed sentences.
Different conversations have different purposes, such as finding information, settling a disagreement, negotiating, or deciding what to do.
summaries.why_it_matters: Arguments influence school rules, public decisions, health choices, and personal relationships. Learning informal logic helps you slow down before accepting or sharing a claim. You can ask what evidence supports it, what assumptions it depends on, and whether the evidence fits the situation. These habits make disagreement more thoughtful without pretending that every question has one simple answer.

important_terms.definition: The study of reasons and conclusions as they appear in everyday speech, writing, debate, and decision-making.
An attempt to support a point of view with reasons, rather than merely expressing disagreement.
A reason given in support of a conclusion.
The claim an argument tries to establish or make more believable.
A claim that is not said aloud but is needed to connect the reasons to the conclusion.
A repeated type of reasoning, such as reasoning from an example or from an expert, that can be tested with questions.
A reasoning mistake or unreliable pattern, although some forms called fallacies may be reasonable in certain situations.
A way of making an argument clear by listing its reasons and conclusion and sometimes drawing their connections.

questions_to_think_about: What makes a reason relevant to a conclusion?
Why might two people judge the same premise differently?
Can an argument use emotion without being irrational?
How could an advertisement make a claim through an image instead of a sentence?
Why might the same argument need to be presented differently to different audiences?
